crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
children.blurb: Pathology detection and scan triage systems examine medical images such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and pathology slides to flag suspicious findings and order cases by urgency.

children.name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
children.blurb: Synthetic imaging from existing scans refers to AI systems that create new medical images derived from one or more prior scans, such as generating a contrast-enhanced CT from a non-contrast study, synthesizing an MRI sequence from another sequence, or producing a pseudo-CT from MRI for radiotherapy planning.

children.name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
children.blurb: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology turn CT and MRI scans into physical, patient-specific replicas of organs, bones, and vascular structures.

children.name: Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement
children.blurb: Point of care ultrasound enhancement covers AI software that helps a clinician acquire, interpret, and act on ultrasound images at the bedside.

children.name: Radiomics
children.blurb: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images such as CT, MRI, and PET scans.

sections.body: Diagnostic imaging and radiology is the part of medicine that turns pictures of the body into decisions about disease, injury and treatment. Artificial intelligence is now used in this field for tasks such as flagging a scan that may contain a bleed, a fracture, a nodule or another urgent finding, and for sorting a long worklist so that the most concerning cases reach a human reader sooner. It also helps create synthetic images from existing scans, build 3D anatomical models for planning and printing, improve point of care ultrasound, and extract quantitative features from images through radiomics. These systems do not replace radiologists or sonographers. They act as a second reader, a triage aid or a measurement tool, and their output still depends on the quality of the input scan and the clinical context. The work is practical, not speculative, and it is already embedded in some reading rooms and emergency departments.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Where the work stands is mixed. Some tasks are well solved in narrow settings, such as detecting certain findings on a specific type of scan when the image quality is good and the population is similar to the training data. Many other tasks remain fragile, including rare diseases, unusual scanners, poor quality images and patients who do not match the original dataset. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 804 scientific models, which shows how much of this field is still research, and it also tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, a reminder that an error in an imaging tool can have serious consequences. The honest limits are clear: these systems can miss findings, can be fooled by artifacts, can inherit bias from their training data, and often cannot explain their reasoning in a way that satisfies a clinician or a regulator. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages reflect the growing effort to test, document and monitor these tools after they reach the clinic.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section divide the work by task and by output. Pathology Detection and Scan Triage is the entry point for readers who want to know how AI finds and ranks urgent findings in a stack of images. Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans covers methods that generate new images from old ones, which can help with training, privacy and rare cases but also raises questions about whether a synthetic image is faithful to the patient. Anatomical Models and 3D Printing shows how imaging data becomes a physical or digital model for surgical planning, device fitting and education. Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement focuses on making bedside ultrasound easier to interpret, especially where a trained specialist is not present. Radiomics is the page for readers who want to turn images into numbers and use those numbers for prediction, and the site's 686 glossary terms can help with the vocabulary along the way.
